strengths: PAPE addresses an important deployment problem: estimating classification performance when production labels are unavailable. Combining target-specific weighted calibration with confidence-based performance estimation is a simple, practically useful approach.

The main evaluation is substantial: 959 model–dataset cases and 36,557 production chunks. PAPE consistently improves over strong baselines, achieving accuracy/AUROC/F1 NMAE of 0.97/0.99/0.90 versus 1.04/1.06/1.07 for importance weighting. The additional TableShift results show similar improvements.

Using the same calibrator for CBPE and the same density-ratio estimator for importance weighting makes these comparisons informative about PAPE’s components. The temporal training/reference/production split is also appropriate for the monitoring application.

The paper clearly connects its approach to CBPE, importance weighting, and multicalibration. Its discussion of concept shift, support mismatch, and dimensionality limitations is candid and useful. No material ethical concern is apparent from the reported public-data experiments.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.2 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider balanced binary X, Y=X, f(X)=X, the usual classification threshold, and c(v)=0.5 for every v. Then c∘f is perfectly calibrated, but Equation (4) estimates accuracy as 0.5 while actual accuracy is 1. Appendix B.2 assumes calibration residuals conditional on the original score f(X), which is stronger than calibration conditional on c(f(X)). This distinction is consequential because the method explicitly permits non-injective regression calibrators. The central error bound and associated unbiasedness claims require stronger assumptions.

The variance comparison in Appendix C analyzes the wrong sampling distribution for importance weighting: Equation (12) samples X from the target distribution while multiplying by p_t/p_s. Unbiased importance weighting instead uses source-distributed samples. The derivation also treats score calibration as establishing correctness probabilities conditional on the full input X, which does not follow. Consequently, the variance comparison and proposed estimator-selection criterion are not established.

Appendix A.1 contains material inconsistencies in the implemented metrics’ specification. Confusion-matrix entries are normalized separately by predicted-positive/negative counts, but Equation (6) subsequently uses them as counts alongside n+. One FN expression is labeled TN, and FPR is written as TN/(TN+FP), which is specificity. These may be transcription errors, but corrected equations and an implementation are needed to resolve whether the reported F1/AUROC results use the intended estimators.

The claim of valid confidence intervals is insufficiently supported. Appendix A.1 explicitly omits interval experiments, and the paper does not establish coverage accounting for learned density ratios and calibration mappings. The population calibration assumptions in the theory are also not shown to hold for the fitted LightGBM pipeline.

The experiments support practical promise more strongly than general robustness under covariate shift. There is no controlled evaluation with known density ratios and verified conditional-label invariance. TableShift combines labeled ID and OoD validation data to fit estimators and combines their test sets, so it does not preserve the standard ID-to-OoD evaluation. The sample-size study covers only one case, and the reported Wilcoxon significance does not explain how dependence among chunks and models sharing data is handled.

Reproducibility and originality need stronger support. No implementation link is provided, and preprocessing, neural-network configuration, and the validation protocol used to select the calibrator are insufficiently specified. The methodological novelty principally lies in integrating established density-ratio estimation, weighted calibration, and CBPE. The empirical gains are worthwhile, but the incorrect central guarantee and unresolved metric specifications outweigh them in the current manuscript.
